idiom_name: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex with the withLock extension (suspending, non-blocking)
implementation_notes: Kotlin offers two policy families with different semantics: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex, whose lock() is a suspending function that parks the coroutine instead of the thread and whose withLock extension is the scoped guard, and the JVM primitives synchronized/ReentrantLock reached through the kotlin.concurrent.withLock extension. The component holds whichever policy was injected, so the abstract Lock class is unnecessary - but the coroutine Mutex changes the colouring of every critical-section function (they must be suspend), while the JVM lock blocks a thread and is the choice when the component is consumed from blocking code or from Java. Prefer the coroutine policy inside a coroutine application, and never hold a JVM lock across a suspension point.
pitfalls: Mutex.withLock protects only coroutines that go through the same Mutex instance; a Mutex created per call provides no exclusion at all.

Holding a kotlinx Mutex across a long blocking call, or a JVM lock across a suspension point, either stalls the dispatcher's thread or leaves the lock's ownership ambiguous - keep critical sections free of suspension apart from the lock itself.
synchronized on the JVM cannot be swapped and blocks a thread, so a component whose policy should be configurable must not reach for it inside its critical sections.

variants.name: JVM ReentrantLock/ReadWriteLock strategy (blocking)
variants.idiom_name: java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock selected per policy with kotlin.concurrent.withLock
variants.implementation_notes: The blocking realization on the JVM: the component holds a java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock (ReentrantLock, or a ReadWriteLock whose read/write locks are handed out per operation) and closes critical sections with the kotlin.concurrent.withLock extension, which acquires and releases in a finally block. Choose it when the component is consumed from Java or from ordinary blocking code, or when a reader/writer policy is needed - kotlinx.coroutines has no read/write Mutex - and accept that a contended lock blocks its thread instead of suspending a coroutine.
pitfalls: ReentrantLock is re-entrant, so an accidental second acquisition through a helper is invisible until profiling shows doubled overhead; keep public methods locking once and _impl methods assuming the lock is held.

Two components each taking their own strategy can still deadlock (A holds a, calls B which takes b); one strategy per component plus a documented acquisition order is the discipline, not the type system.
Taking a JDK lock inside a coroutine blocks the dispatcher thread; confine such components to Dispatchers.IO or keep them entirely on the blocking path.
